name: Total Crop Yield from Area
description: Calculates total crop production by multiplying the field area A by the yield per hectare y, giving the total harvest in tonnes for the whole field.
notes: Area must be in hectares to match the per-hectare yield so the units cancel to tonnes. Assumes uniform yield across the field; patchy fields give only an average estimate.

name: Harvest Index
description: Computes the harvest index, the ratio of economic (harvested) yield Ye to total biological yield Yb. It expresses what fraction of the crop's biomass ends up as the useful product.
notes: Dimensionless and between 0 and 1; Ye and Yb must share units so they cancel. Biological yield is the total above-ground (or whole-plant) biomass, so it should exceed the economic yield.

name: Seeding Rate (kg/ha)
description: Determines the seeding rate in kilograms per hectare needed to reach a target plant density. It adjusts the target density D upward for germination G and purity P, then scales by the thousand-kernel weight TKW.
notes: G and P are fractions below 1, which raise the rate to compensate for losses. TKW is grams per 1000 seeds; the /100 factor reconciles plants/m² and grams into kg/ha. Field emergence may be lower than lab germination.

name: Plant Population Density
description: Calculates the number of plants per hectare from the planting geometry. It divides the 10000 m² in a hectare by the area each plant occupies, the product of row spacing rs and in-row spacing ps.
notes: rs and ps must be in metres so rs×ps is m² per plant and the result is plants per hectare. Gives the theoretical stand at full emergence, before thinning or seedling loss.

name: Nitrogen Fertilizer Requirement
description: Estimates the nitrogen fertilizer needed for a target yield. It takes crop N demand Y×u, subtracts the soil N supply Ns, then divides by the N use efficiency nue to account for fertilizer not taken up.
notes: u is N uptake per tonne of yield; nue (a fraction below 1) inflates the requirement to cover losses. All terms should be in kg N per hectare. A negative or zero result means soil supply already meets demand.

name: Fertilizer Product Rate from Nutrient
description: Converts a required nutrient amount into the physical fertilizer product rate. It divides the nutrient requirement Nreq by the nutrient grade expressed as a fraction (gr/100), giving product mass per hectare.
notes: gr is the nutrient percentage by mass on the product label (e.g. 46 for urea), so it is divided by 100. Result and Nreq share the mass-per-area unit. Applies to a single nutrient grade.

name: Crop Evapotranspiration (Kc Method)
description: Computes crop evapotranspiration by the crop-coefficient method, multiplying the reference evapotranspiration ET0 by the crop coefficient Kc. It gives the crop's daily water use under standard conditions.
notes: Kc varies with crop type and growth stage and can exceed 1 at peak canopy. ET0 and the result share the same depth-per-day unit. Represents water demand under well-watered, non-stressed conditions.

name: Reference Evapotranspiration (Hargreaves)
description: Estimates reference evapotranspiration with the Hargreaves equation, using extraterrestrial radiation Ra, mean temperature Tm and the square root of the daily temperature range (Tx−Tn) as a proxy for solar and humidity effects.
notes: Temperatures are in degrees Celsius and Ra must be expressed in the same depth-per-day units as the result. Requires Tx greater than Tn so the square root is real. It is an empirical approximation, less accurate than Penman-Monteith.

name: Net Irrigation Requirement
description: Computes the net irrigation requirement as the crop evapotranspiration ETc minus the effective rainfall Pe. It gives the water depth that irrigation must supply after accounting for useful rain.
notes: ETc and Pe must be in the same depth unit (mm). A negative result means rainfall exceeds crop demand, so no irrigation is needed. This is the net depth, before dividing by application efficiency.

name: Gross Irrigation Requirement
description: Converts the net irrigation depth into the gross amount that must be applied, dividing the net depth Net by the application efficiency Ea to account for water lost during delivery and distribution.
notes: Ea is a fraction below 1, so the gross depth always exceeds the net. It captures losses like runoff, deep percolation and evaporation. Net and the result share the same depth unit.

name: Irrigation Volume (per Field)
description: Calculates the total irrigation water volume for a field. It multiplies the water application depth d (in mm) by the field area A (in hectares), with a factor of 10 to convert mm×ha into cubic metres.
notes: The factor 10 arises because 1 mm over 1 hectare equals 10 m³. Depth must be in millimetres and area in hectares for the result to be cubic metres.

name: Effective Rainfall (USDA Approximation)
description: Estimates the effective (crop-usable) portion of rainfall with the USDA-SCS formula P×(125−0.2×P)/125. It reduces total rainfall to reflect losses from runoff and deep percolation as rainfall increases.
notes: This monthly approximation is valid roughly up to P around 250 mm, beyond which the parabola turns down unphysically. P and the result are in millimetres. It is empirical and region-dependent.

name: Growing Degree Days (Daily)
description: Computes daily growing degree days as the average of the day's maximum and minimum temperatures minus the crop base temperature Tb. It quantifies the day's accumulated heat available for crop development.
notes: Temperatures are in degrees Celsius. A negative result should normally be set to zero, since no growth accrues below the base temperature. Some methods also cap Tx at an upper threshold before averaging.

name: Crop Water Use Efficiency
description: Divides crop yield by the volume of water used to produce it, giving the mass of harvest obtained per cubic metre of water. Higher values mean each unit of water generates more yield.
notes: Water W should count all inputs considered (irrigation plus effective rainfall, depending on definition); using only irrigation water changes the meaning. Keep units consistent, here kg per m3.

name: Leaf Area Index
description: Ratio of the total one-sided leaf area of a canopy to the ground area it covers, giving a dimensionless index of canopy density. A value of 4 means four square metres of leaf per square metre of ground.
notes: Both areas must use the same unit so the result is dimensionless. Convention typically uses one-sided leaf area; mixing in both leaf sides doubles the index.

name: Available Water Capacity (Soil Profile)
description: Estimates the depth of plant-available water held in a root zone as the difference between field capacity and permanent wilting point (as volume percent) multiplied by root zone depth. The result is an equivalent water depth in millimetres.
notes: FC and PWP are volumetric water contents in percent, so dividing by 100 converts them to a fraction. Depth d must be in millimetres for the result to come out in millimetres.

name: Soil Bulk Density
description: Divides the mass of oven-dry soil by the total volume of the sample (including pore space) to give the soil bulk density. It indicates soil compaction, with higher values meaning denser, more compacted soil.
notes: Use oven-dry soil mass, not moist mass, and the total sample volume including pores. Typical mineral soils range roughly 1.1 to 1.6 g/cm3; very high values suggest compaction.

name: Soil Porosity
description: Calculates the fraction of soil volume made up of pore space as one minus the ratio of bulk density to particle density. A result of 0.5 means half the soil volume is pores (air or water).
notes: Both densities must share the same unit. Particle density must exceed bulk density, so the result stays between 0 and 1; multiply by 100 for percent porosity.

name: Feed Conversion Ratio
description: Divides the mass of feed consumed by the weight gained by the animal, giving the amount of feed needed per unit of body-mass gain. Lower values indicate more efficient conversion of feed into growth.
notes: Feed and gain must use the same mass unit so the ratio is dimensionless. Measure both over the same period; unlike most efficiency measures, a smaller FCR is better.

name: Average Daily Gain
description: Divides the total weight gained (final minus initial) by the number of days on feed to give the average daily weight gain of an animal. It expresses growth rate as mass added per day.
notes: It gives an average over the whole period and hides day-to-day variation. Keep weights in the same unit; the result here is kilograms per day.

name: Livestock Stocking Density
description: Divides the number of animals by the pasture area to give the stocking density, the number of head grazing per hectare. Higher values mean more animals concentrated on the same land.
notes: This is a simple head count per area and does not account for animal size or forage supply; use animal units or carrying capacity for grazing management decisions.

name: Dry Matter Intake
description: Estimates an animal's daily dry matter intake as a given percentage of its body weight. For example, 2.5 percent of a 600 kg animal gives 15 kg of dry matter per day.
notes: The percentage p is entered as a number (2.5 for 2.5 percent) and divided by 100 internally. It estimates dry matter, not as-fed feed, which contains moisture.

name: Grazing Days Available
description: Estimates how many days a herd can graze a pasture by dividing the usable forage (dry matter per hectare times area times utilization rate) by the herd's total daily intake. The result is grazing days for the whole herd.
notes: Utilization rate U is a fraction between 0 and 1 accounting for forage not eaten or trampled. It assumes no regrowth during the period, so it underestimates for growing pastures.

name: Seed Germination Percentage
description: Divides the number of germinated seeds by the total number tested and multiplies by 100 to give the germination percentage of a seed lot. It indicates seed viability and lot quality.
notes: Count germinated seeds under standard test conditions over a fixed period. The result cannot exceed 100 percent; germinated seeds must not be more than the total tested.

name: Spray Application Volume
description: Multiplies the field area by the application rate per hectare to give the total spray volume needed to treat the field. It tells how much spray solution to prepare for the whole area.
notes: The rate r must be per hectare and the area A in hectares so the units cancel to litres. This is total mix volume, not the amount of active ingredient.

name: Available Nitrogen from Manure
description: Multiplies the mass of manure applied, its total nitrogen content per tonne, and an availability factor to estimate the nitrogen actually available to the crop. It gives plant-available N in kilograms.
notes: The availability factor (0 to 1) reflects the share of total N released in the season; the rest is organically bound and slowly mineralized. Keep manure mass and N content in matching tonne units.

name: Lime Requirement (Buffer Method)
description: Estimates the amount of lime needed to raise soil pH by multiplying the pH increase wanted (target minus current) by a soil buffer factor and a conversion factor. The result is lime rate in kilograms per hectare.
notes: The buffer factor reflects the soil's resistance to pH change and depends on a buffer test; it is not universal. Results are approximate and vary with liming material quality and soil type.

name: Dry Matter Yield
description: Converts a fresh (as-harvested) weight of forage or crop into dry matter yield by applying its measured dry matter percentage, DM_yield = fresh_weight*(dry_matter_percent/100).
notes: Dry matter percentage varies widely with crop, maturity, and moisture at cutting, so it should be measured or sampled rather than assumed. Fresh weight and dry matter yield share the same mass unit.

name: Irrigation Application Efficiency
description: Computes irrigation application efficiency, Ea = useful_water_applied/total_water_applied*100, the percentage of applied irrigation water that is actually stored in the crop root zone rather than lost to runoff, deep percolation, or evaporation.
notes: Both volumes must share the same unit so they cancel before the percentage conversion. Higher values indicate a more efficient irrigation system or scheduling; well-managed drip systems can exceed 90%.
